principles: DONE must be fail-closed on gate-consumed structured evidence, not prose claims.
Self-host Lattice core needs stronger release assurance than ordinary external projects by default.
External projects must remain configurable and must not inherit Orchestrate-specific full-suite cost unless they opt in.
Validation evidence must be bound to current HEAD/material/story files so stale green runs cannot unlock DONE.
drivers: Prevent false DONE when configured lattice validate subset passes but full root npm test would fail.
Keep normal DEV/TEST feedback fast enough for story iteration.
Make the future implementation mechanically testable with explicit artifacts and row ids.
Preserve 3-round/2-host review discipline for high-risk lifecycle gate changes.

options.name: A: Add root npm test directly to validate.commands
pros: Uses the existing lattice validate and test-evidence path.
cons: Makes every validate expensive, including normal REVIEW to TEST movement.
Does not distinguish project-level validation from self-host DONE/release assurance.
Could make external users copy an Orchestrate-specific policy into unrelated projects.

options.name: B: Add DONE/release-required validation profile with hash-bound evidence
pros: Separates fast project validation from DONE/release closure evidence.
Lets Orchestrate require root npm test while external projects opt in or configure their own equivalent.
Can expose a dedicated DONE row and clear stale/failing runbook.
cons: Requires schema, runner, artifact, done-oracle, docs, and smoke updates.
Needs careful migration for in-flight stories and cached test evidence.

options.name: C: Rely on pre-push or CI for full npm test
pros: Keeps current story lifecycle mostly unchanged.
cons: Does not fix local DONE semantics; stories can still merge to local main while full tests are red.
Push/CI feedback arrives after Lattice has already claimed DONE.
Current pre-push does not run root npm test anyway.

chosen: B: Add DONE/release-required validation profile with hash-bound evidence
rationale: Choose a dedicated DONE/release-required validation profile because the bug is specifically a closure assurance gap, not a normal fast feedback gap. The plan should require root npm test for this self-host repository while preserving configurable project-native validation for external users.

preMortem.scenario: Implementation makes every lattice validate run execute full npm test.
preMortem.trigger: The fix only appends npm test to validate.commands.
preMortem.consequence: Normal development becomes slow, agents avoid validate, and external projects inherit self-host cost.
preMortem.mitigation: Define a separate DONE/release profile and keep normal validate.commands behavior intact unless a project opts into stronger policy.

preMortem.scenario: DONE accepts stale full-suite evidence after material changes.
preMortem.trigger: The full-suite artifact records pass/fail but not HEAD/material/storyFilesHash.
preMortem.consequence: A previous green npm test can unlock DONE for a changed story.
preMortem.mitigation: Require the same freshness model as test-evidence: current HEAD/material/storyFilesHash and explicit stale row failure.

preMortem.scenario: The plan creates prompt-only policy with no gate consumer.
preMortem.trigger: Docs say full npm test is required but no done-oracle/process-fact/validation runner consumes it.
preMortem.consequence: Agents still merge with subset evidence because the mechanical gate is unchanged.
preMortem.mitigation: Require implementation touchpoints for schema, verifier/runner, process fact registry, done-oracle row, tests, and docs.

preMortem.scenario: 3-round/2-host review is treated as a doc checkbox rather than current-material evidence.
preMortem.trigger: Host verdicts are recorded before final implementation or without material hash binding.
preMortem.consequence: High-risk gate changes get stale or duplicate review assurance.
preMortem.mitigation: Plan mandates review escalation/host verdicts over final material hash and re-attestation after material changes.
